Norton Sound-Port Clarence Salmon Season Summary

October 14, 2026

Forrest Bowers, Acting Director

Doug Vincent-Lang, Commissioner

Nome Office Nome, AK 99762

Juneau, AK 99811-5526

For Immediate Release: October 14, 2026

CONTACT: Kevin Clark or Luke Henslee Norton Sound Area Manager & Asst. Manager (907) 443-5167 or (800) 560-2271

2026 NORTON SOUND-PORT CLARENCE SALMON SEASON SUMMARY

In 2026, salmon returns to the Norton Sound District supported commercial fisheries targeting chum and coho salmon in the coastal waters of Subdistricts 2–6 with other species harvested incidentally. The total salmon harvest was the highest in the last 4 years but was below the most recent 5-year average. The total value of the fishery was near the recent average, though commercial effort in Norton Sound was the lowest in 20 years. There were no emergency orders restricting subsistence salmon fishing except for Chinook salmon conservation restrictions in Subdistricts 5 and 6 that have been enacted since 2024. Salmon returns varied greatly by species and by subdistrict, but most escapement goals were achieved. This summary contains preliminary numbers that will be updated in subsequent reports.

COMMERCIAL SALMON FISHERY

Salmon returns to Norton Sound varied, with chum salmon achieving all but 1 goal, pink salmon achieving goals were achieved at the Kwiniuk River in Subdistrict 3, but North River tower in Subdistrict 6 ceased operations before the coho salmon escapement goal could be met. The sockeye salmon escapement goal in the Port Clarence District was met for the 3rd year in a row. Throughout Norton Sound, pink salmon returns were above average, except in Subdistrict 1 where the pink salmon goal at Nome River was not achieved.

The 2026 Norton Sound commercial harvest of 48,700 salmon was below average, though the fishery value of $320,657 was near the recent 5-year average (Table 1). The commercial effort of 72 permits was the lowest since 2007 and ranged from 5 fishermen in Subdistrict 4 to 28 fishermen in Subdistrict 6 (Table 2). Chum salmon catch of 24,730 fish was double the recent 5-year average and the coho salmon catch of 13,639 fish was near the recent 5-year average (Table 3).

One salmon buyer operated in the region in 2026, Norton Sound Seafood Products (NSSP), with the Unalakleet processing plant being the buyer’s main base of operations. NSSP also processed some commercial salmon catch at their plant in Nome. There were no catcher-seller permits registered with the department in 2026. Prices paid per pound in 2026 were $2.20 for sockeye salmon, $1.90 for coho salmon, $0.75 for chum salmon, and $0.35 for pink salmon. The price for all species was the same as in 2025. Chinook salmon were not purchased by NSSP in 2026.

SUBSISTENCE SALMON FISHERY

Subsistence salmon fishermen in the Port Clarence District and Norton Sound Subdistricts 1–3 are required to possess a subsistence permit for each household that fishes in these locations. The permit holder records

the harvest method and the catch in numbers of fish by species for each day fished. Permits are due back to the department by October 6th each year. In southern Norton Sound, census surveys in the communities of Koyuk, Shaktoolik, and Unalakleet estimate subsistence harvest and effort.

In the Port Clarence District, catch limits for Pilgrim River sockeye were waived on July 4 when escapement objectives were projected to be achieved. Due to Chinook salmon conservation concerns, the department closed subsistence fishing in the marine and fresh waters of Subdistricts 5 and 6 starting on June 15 and allowed only limited subsistence fishing targeting non-salmon species in freshwaters. Subsistence opportunities were liberalized on June 30, allowing beach seining with the non-retention of Chinook salmon. On July 16 marine waters of Subdistricts 5 and 6 were open to gillnet gear with mesh size restricted to 6 inches or less, and fresh waters were open to subsistence gillnet fishing by emergency order on July 22.

Subsistence harvest data is collected in the months after the end of the salmon season and final estimates are not available for this summary. However, anecdotal evidence from fishermen in the region indicate that most residents were able to meet their salmon needs in the 2026 season. Subsistence fishermen in Port Clarence and the Pilgrim River used beach seines and set gillnets to harvest sockeye salmon. Northern Norton Sound subsistence users reported success catching chum, pink, and coho in marine and freshwater using gillnets and rod and reel. Fishermen in southern Norton Sound were able to put away salmon using beach seine methods to catch chum and pinks early in the season and set gillnets to catch coho salmon after restrictions were lifted.

SEASON SUMMARY BY SUBDISTRICT

Nome - Subdistrict 1

Based on low salmon returns in the previous year, a conservative management approach was taken in Subdistrict 1 for the 2026 season. Lackluster escapement counts for chum salmon early in the season precluded commercial periods, although escapement goals were eventually met in the Snake and Nome rivers west of Cape Nome. East of Cape Nome, chum escapement to the Eldorado River was at historical lows in 2026. Coho salmon escapement monitored by projects in Subdistrict 1 was low and did not indicate a harvestable surplus. Ultimately, there were no commercial fishing periods in Subdistrict 1 in 2026.

Salmon runs were below average in the Nome Subdistrict. Nome River pink salmon did not achieve escapement objectives in 2026, and Eldorado chum salmon escapement was well below the goal range of 4,400–14,200 fish (Table 4). Weir operations on the Nome River were consistent for most of the season, until high water forced the end of the project on September 10. The Snake River weir ran intermittently until the project ceased operations on August 23. Coho salmon passage was below average at assessment projects when high water events caused the weirs to become inoperable. Aerial surveys flown of some Subdistrict 1 rivers on September 22 indicated lackluster escapement abundance of coho salmon.

Golovin - Subdistrict 2

There were 14 commercial fishing periods directed at chum or coho salmon with gillnets restricted to 6 inches or smaller mesh size. There were 14 permit holders that fished this year, which was near the historical average of 15 permits. Catch rates in the chum salmon commercial fishery were generally above the longterm historical average and escapement was near the 75th percentile of historical escapements. The

2

October 14, 2026

commercial coho salmon fishery started on July 29 and catch rates for the season were near average. The commercial harvest was 1,054 sockeye, 1,676 chum, and 11,485 coho salmon (Table 2).

Niukluk River tower operations ran fairly consistently in 2026 but was pulled early due to high waters. The project started counting on June 24 and operated until high water events put counts on hold from August 4–13 and ultimately caused the project to end early on August 21. The preliminary counts from the tower are 174 Chinook, 41,326 chum, 1,073,361 pink, 558 sockeye, and 523 coho salmon (Table 4).

Elim - Subdistrict 3

Due to low returns in previous years, the department took a cautious approach to scheduling chum salmon fishery openers in Subdistrict 3. There were 14 commercial fishing periods targeting chum or coho salmon with gillnets restricted to 6 inches or smaller mesh size. The 18 permit holders that fished in 2026 matched the recent 5-year average of 18 permits. Harvest rates for chum salmon during the first fishing period on July 7 were above average and early Kwiniuk River tower chum salmon estimates were projected to meet escapement objectives. This led the department to eventually schedule two 48-hour fishing periods a week until management switched to coho salmon on July 29. Fishing performance during periods directed to coho salmon were generally near average and the escapement goal of 4,400 was achieved in the third week of August. The commercial harvest totaled 906 sockeye, 5,315 chum, 5,509 pink, and 2,276 coho salmon (Table 2).

Of the four established Kwiniuk River escapement goals, three were achieved in 2026. Chinook salmon passage was below the escapement goal of 250 fish for the sixth year in a row. Chum salmon passage met the escapement goal range of 9,100–32,600. The pink salmon escapement goal threshold of 8,400 fish was exceeded. The coho salmon tower-based goal of 4,400 fish, which was newly established at the Board of Fish meeting in November 2025, was achieved. Escapement counts at the Kwiniuk River tower were 63 Chinook, 16,809 chum, 746,600 pink, 300 sockeye, and 6,123 coho salmon (Table 4).

Norton Bay - Subdistrict 4

Subdistrict 4 was managed in conjunction with Subdistricts 2 and 3 in 2026 based on fishing performance. There were 14 commercial fishing periods with gillnets restricted to 6-inch mesh or less. Commercial harvest totaled 140 sockeye, 1,768 chum, 435 pink, and 503 coho salmon, which were all well below average. Effort was sporadic throughout the season and only 5 permits fished, which is below the average participation of 11 permits.

A counting tower on the Ungalik River operated in 2026 but was limited by high water with periods of missed or incomplete escapement and counts should be considered a minimum. Escapement estimates were 36 Chinook salmon, 8,859 chum, 445,879 pink, 276 coho, and 0 sockeye salmon (Table 4).

Shaktoolik and Unalakleet - Subdistricts 5 and 6

Shaktoolik and Unalakleet subdistricts share a common commercial fishing boundary, and management actions typically encompass both subdistricts as salmon intermingle in the marine waters of Subdistricts 5 and 6. In 2026, poor Chinook runs in both subdistricts caused the department to forgo early season salmon openings to allow for additional escapement. Commercial fishing started on July 24, and there were 9 commercial fishing periods targeting coho salmon with gillnets restricted to 6 inches or smaller mesh size. Catch rates for coho salmon were near historical averages. There were 9 permit holders that fished in the

3

October 14, 2026

Shaktoolik Subdistrict and in Unalakleet there were 28 permit holders. The Shaktoolik commercial harvest was 421 sockeye, 2,015 chum, 253 pink and 2,383 coho salmon. The Unalakleet commercial harvest was 389 sockeye, 4,147 chum, 1,224 pink and 6,799 coho salmon (Table 2).

There are two counting tower projects in these subdistricts located on the Shaktoolik and North rivers. The Shaktoolik River counting tower started operations on June 26. However, due to high, turbid water the tower operated sporadically during the 2026 season and counted 411 Chinook salmon, 8,067 chum, 349,974 pink, and 1,701 coho salmon. The North River tower began on June 17 and operated more consistently than other projects in southern Norton Sound but still had a long period of unmonitored escapement due to high waters between August 4–12 and operations ended early on August 22. The North River Chinook salmon escapement of 399 fish was well below the lower end of the escapement goal range of 1,200–2,600 fish (Table 4). Other salmon counts at North River tower were 2,787 chum, 469,591 pink, 321 coho, and 9 sockeye salmon.

Port Clarence District

Port Clarence District is home to the furthest north sockeye salmon run in the state. Each year, the seasonal subsistence catch limit is 25 sockeye salmon per household and the department can raise the limit if returns are projected to exceed escapement needs. An early, strong run of sockeye led the department to waive household sockeye limits on July 4. The Pilgrim River weir count of 34,232 sockeye salmon exceeded the escapement threshold of 6,400 fish. To allow for a commercial fishery an escapement of 30,000 sockeye salmon must be projected in the Pilgrim River. Sockeye escapement was adequate for commercial fishing in 2026, but market interest has not existed in over 10 years.
